Daniel’s sketch hides a large assumption: that “feeling the rhythm” is a localized function that will reveal itself as a single frequency match between stimulus and brain signal. In practice, what a Fourier transform reliably detects is *entrainment* (neural activity phase-locking to periodic input), which is not identical to the subjective experience of beat or groove. A listener can show steady-state responses to an amplitude-modulated sound without perceiving a beat, and conversely can perceive a beat even when the acoustic signal is syncopated or missing onsets—suggesting the key computation is partly *predictive* and top‑down rather than just stimulus-following. This is why much of the beat-perception literature emphasizes a perception–action loop and internal oscillatory models rather than “a rhythm center” (e.g., the dynamical attending tradition and work surveyed in Aniruddh Patel’s [*Music, Language, and the Brain*](https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674027813/music-language-and-the-brain)).

A second blind spot is methodological: “Fourier transform on brain activity” sounds clean, but different measurement tools change what “frequency” even means. EEG/MEG can show frequency-tagged responses but has limited spatial precision; fMRI has spatial resolution but is too slow to capture tempo directly, so it tends to pick up indirect correlates (effort, prediction error, motor planning). Without an explicit behavioral readout (beat-tapping accuracy, phase correction, perceived groove ratings), the experiment risks correlating tempo with generic arousal, attention, or covert movement. If Daniel wants an “area in charge,” he likely ends up in the well-known network involving auditory cortex plus motor-related circuitry—especially basal ganglia and cerebellum—because beat perception is tightly coupled to timing and action even when the subject is still. The more interesting conclusion, if he leans into it, is not a rhythm module but a distributed predictive timing system whose signatures shift with task, tempo range, and musical structure.
